title: Polarisation Sensitive (PS)-Optical Coherence Tomography for the Diagnosis of Cancer and Other Diseases of the Hepatobiliary and Gastrointestinal System
summary:
In cancer surgery, it is essential to remove the tumour completely while preserving as much healthy tissue as possible. To ensure this, tissue samples must be repeatedly sent to the pathology department during the operation and examined there – a process that can be time-consuming and has technical limitations.

This study investigates whether a new imaging method – optical coherence tomography (OCT) – can help to assess tissue more rapidly and precisely. The OCT technique works similarly to ultrasound, but uses light instead of sound waves, providing high-resolution images of the tissue without causing any damage. In combination with artificial intelligence (AI), the system is intended to automatically detect whether tissue is healthy or pathologically altered.

What happens in practice?
The tissue removed during your operation will be examined for a few minutes using the OCT system before it is processed in the pathology department. This device is located directly within the pathology laboratory, meaning there is no delay whatsoever to your diagnostic report. The tissue is then examined histologically in the usual manner.

What changes for you as a patient?
Nothing. The operation, the follow-up care and all further treatment steps remain completely unchanged. No additional tissue will be taken. Your hospital stay will not be extended.

Where is the study being conducted?
The study is being conducted at the University Hospital RWTH Aachen, in close collaboration between the Department of Surgery, the Department of Pathology and the Fraunhofer Institute for Production Technology (IPT). It is planned to run over a period of 5 years.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Adult patients (≥ 18 years) undergoing gastrointestinal (GI), hepatopancreaticobiliary (HPB), transplantation or thyroid surgery
- Ability to provide written informed consent
- Patients with both malignant and non-malignant conditions
Exclusion criteria:
- Inability or refusal to provide written informed consent
- Patients under 18 years of age
- Patients undergoing emergency surgery
